The mechanics are that of an uninspired phishing simulation. Which contrasts with the narrative framing of "you are a really dangerous nerd". I feel like a game like grayhack or hacknet is fit more for that framing. Even the tutorial was highly boring for me. Maybe the story you get after the tutorial is good, but i didn't get that far.

Well you see I understand that a game would need some embellishing and effects to sell the power fantasy and divert from the seams of skipping real life logic, but the choices this game made regarding that front makes me see those seams harder rather than immersing me in the fantasy.

very light spoilers ahead from the first ten minutes of gameplay(tutorial and intro)

First, i got whiplashed right off with the phrase "our company got a BILLION BYTES of customer data". Holy shit dude, that's a lot for a large tech company at the like 90s maybe. Not for the presented "everyone is glued to their phones using social media" setting.  Less than a god damn gigabyte, basically three times less than the space this game takes on your ssd.

Then we got the random code prompts opening every time we copy the details from the browser about someone's facebook account to some contacts type information collection software. It feels less hackery and more like the "linux users when x" memes, because why would code prompts open when you are just copy pasting something from one gui to some other gui.


Then apparently we have access to the data of almost all citizens in our nation through the company database software. For some reason when accessing the data we or the software executes almost totally unrelated linux commands, which i don't understand why since it is not a cli tool but poses as a professional corpo gui software, but i guess the company in the story fired the user interface designer/programmer before they finished their job.

Then there is the password "cracker" software. Except this game's version makes me feel like a loser script kiddie the most. All you do is fill in a bunch of details you gathered from the dude's social media page, and the "cracker" spits out some password guess with very few amount of characters based on the entered information. And somehow it's correct like it's some oracle.

It reminds me of that one CheeseParade skit where the guy goes "He's not a hacker, he's a password guesser", and then the guy proceeds to get locked out of the system for inputting the wrong password since it was a guess based on a whim.

Also the OS apparently can't handle a bunch of high speed showcase of cyber security news, crashes and has to restart, which felt like a funny unintentional commentary on the ram shortage crisis. That was the most fun part of the game for me. 

Anyways, so if you like an overly dressed up phishing simulator with seemingly nice worldbuilding and perhaps a good story if you ignore the technical knowledge shortcomings of the writers here and there, maybe its your thing, Otherwise, nah.

I really enjoyed this game. It's not perfect; there is repetitive work per case (sleuthing, hacking) that some might find annoying but really is the basis of the gameplay, and mini-games that has high demands in terms of being able to read quickly and solve problems on the dot. You need to pay attention to detail to get each case done, and every case leads you to ponder if you are doing the right thing.
I had no problem playing the game in English, the occasional hickup in translation or words spelled slightly wrong is not game breaking at all.

The timed events (mini-games) are the worst parts of the game, and some of them give you very little time but lots of info to read through. Most often you play under high pressure and the hints (or even evidence) hidden in plain text can be poor. Failing some of the puzzles ("mini-games") can set you back several minutes and you need to click through a lot of repetitive screens to try again, and some things you can't even skip.
The internet sleuthing part is really restrictive, as sometimes you may search for something but get zero results when it makes no sense. Later in the game, the same search phrase might yield results.
This is too restrictive and doesn't make sense in an investigative game.

If you manage to push through it all, you will be relieved and maybe a little confused, but you will have learned of a complex plot woven together with I'd say 95% success. You also realize the game is trying to tell us how brutal and unfair life can be, which really felt like a blow to the stomach. Without giving any spoiles I'd say if you already feel traumatized by real world events, this game might not be for you. 

All in all, I might sound negative in my review but I had lots of fun. The feeling from finding important clues and solving puzzles before the timer runs out are real dopamine hits. If you enjoy puzzle games and piecing together stories, you might have just as much fun as I did.  I'll be checking out the next game for sure.

Cyber Manhunt is a unique and unsettling narrative-driven puzzle game that places players in the morally murky role of a professional hacker. Developed by Aluba Studio and available on Steam, the game presents itself as a cyber-investigation simulator, mixing detective gameplay with social engineering, data mining, and psychological manipulation. While its interface is minimalist, the themes it explores—digital privacy, online harassment, data vulnerability, and the ethics of surveillance—are far from simple. It’s a modern thriller that unfolds not through action-packed sequences or traditional storytelling, but by letting players piece together lives through clues scattered across emails, social media, and digital records.

Set in a near-future version of our own internet-saturated society, Cyber Manhunt casts the player as an operative for an organization known as "SIVA," which conducts cyber investigations for corporations and government agencies. The game is structured around individual cases, each with its own set of objectives, suspects, and twists. What starts as routine data gathering—finding an email address, uncovering a password, identifying a workplace—quickly escalates into complex moral dilemmas. The deeper you dig into someone’s digital footprint, the more invasive your methods become, forcing you to reckon with the consequences of your virtual actions.

The core gameplay is rooted in investigation and logic puzzles, but what sets Cyber Manhunt apart is how immersive and believable its digital world feels. You spend much of your time trawling through fake but convincingly designed social media platforms, browsing private messages, scanning photos for hidden clues, and exploiting psychological weaknesses to manipulate individuals. The game offers a variety of tools: phishing attacks, password crackers, facial recognition programs, and psychological profiling software, all of which mimic real-world hacking techniques without becoming too technical or inaccessible. The interface, while simple—a desktop environment filled with windows and tabs—creates an atmosphere of quiet tension, as every click feels like crossing an ethical line.

What makes the experience so impactful is the human element. The stories you uncover are deeply personal and often tragic. You’re not just solving abstract puzzles; you’re uncovering infidelities, financial struggles, secrets, traumas, and vulnerabilities. Each case dives into topical issues like revenge porn, cyberbullying, workplace exploitation, doxxing, and the fine line between whistleblowing and invasion of privacy. As the player progresses, the narrative becomes darker and more morally ambiguous. The writing is sharp, and the character development—despite being limited to text, photos, and online profiles—is emotionally resonant. The game challenges you to not only solve a case, but also to reflect on what justice means in a digital age.

Visually, the game keeps things stripped down to focus on content. The UI mimics a clean, modern operating system with elements like chat windows, fake browser tabs, file systems, and message threads. Character portraits and photo attachments are stylized but grounded in realism, helping reinforce the immersion. The visual design cleverly avoids unnecessary distractions, making it easier to focus on parsing clues and tracking connections. Sound design also plays a subtle but important role—keyboard clicks, notification pings, and ambient background noise enhance the feeling of being locked into a high-stakes hacking operation, with minimal music to keep the mood tense and subdued.

One of the most compelling aspects of Cyber Manhunt is how it encourages nonlinear thinking. Often, you’ll need to piece together multiple fragments of information—dates, IP addresses, usernames, workplace gossip, even innocuous photos—to gain access to the next layer of information. The satisfaction of finally cracking a password or realizing a key detail hidden in plain sight is genuinely rewarding. This emphasis on deduction and intuition makes it more engaging than a traditional point-and-click adventure or dialogue-based detective game.

The game isn’t without its limitations. Its structure, while immersive, can sometimes become repetitive in later cases if you're not invested in the unfolding narrative. Some puzzles lean too heavily on trial and error or obscure details, which may frustrate players who prefer more explicit logic. Occasionally, the text-based nature of the game can become a bit overwhelming, especially in later chapters when multiple message threads and platforms must be monitored simultaneously. Additionally, while the game offers strong storytelling, it doesn’t provide much player agency in how outcomes unfold; you’re largely executing a script with little room to change the moral arc of a case.

Still, Cyber Manhunt thrives on the strength of its atmosphere, writing, and relevance. In an age where personal data is a currency and social media has become both weapon and witness, the game’s scenarios hit uncomfortably close to home. It manages to be entertaining, thought-provoking, and disturbing all at once. Each case plays like a mini cyber-thriller, and the emotional weight of the characters’ stories lingers long after the investigation is over. Few games tackle the modern digital landscape with such a grounded and incisive lens.

Overall, Cyber Manhunt is a compelling blend of investigation, narrative, and social commentary. It’s a rare kind of game that treats its players like intelligent observers and asks difficult questions without offering easy answers. For those intrigued by ethical dilemmas, digital privacy, and the psychological impacts of technology, it offers a focused, meaningful experience unlike much else on Steam. It’s not just about solving puzzles—it’s about understanding the cost of digital omniscience and asking yourself whether you’ve gone too far, even when the job is done.

Rating: 8/10

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 305:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆☆ (8/10)

[i]Cyber Manhunt [/i]casts you as a hired hacker working for a shady tech company, diving deep into people’s digital footprints to expose secrets, manipulate outcomes, or destroy lives—depending on who’s paying. It’s a detective game wrapped in social commentary, mixing real-world open-source intelligence tools with a sharp narrative focus on privacy, morality, and the commodification of personal information. The experience is slick, addictive, and surprisingly emotionally charged, even as it drags you through increasingly uncomfortable territory.

🟢 [b]Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*] Clever mechanics that feel grounded and authentic. Each case involves scouring fake websites, piecing together social media data, inspecting photo metadata, and using context clues to crack security questions or passwords. It feels grounded in real techniques used by journalists, investigators, and malicious actors alike. Unlike many “hacker” games that default to flashy visuals and techno-babble, Cyber Manhunt leans into how frighteningly simple it can be to uncover personal details with just a little determination and context.

[*] Great UI. The in-game interface mimics a functioning operating system, complete with fake search engines, chat logs, financial apps, and internal company software. It’s clean, easy to navigate, and does a fantastic job of making you feel like you’re living inside a terminal window for hours. The interface becomes second nature quickly, allowing you to forget you're playing a game and focus entirely on the task of investigation.

[*]Complex moral themes. Rather than relying on one overarching conspiracy (though that's part of the game!), the game gives you a series of smaller, more intimate cases each one touching on different themes like revenge porn, mental illness, cyberbullying, or whistleblowing. What’s impressive is how effectively the game conveys the emotional stakes of these narratives through documents and data alone. You often start a case thinking someone’s in the wrong, only to slowly learn they were a victim all along.

[*] Creative twist on detective work. In many cases, you’ll impersonate people, craft fake identities, send phishing messages, or push emotionally manipulative texts to provoke responses from characters. It’s unsettling how good it feels to “win” a case this way, and that’s part of the point. The game forces you to reckon with your own sense of detachment—how far are you willing to go when the consequences aren’t real?
[/list]

🌐 [b]Cons:[/b]
[*] Can get predictable. While the first few investigations feel novel and rewarding, the structure doesn’t evolve much as you progress. Nearly every case involves the same general process: comb social media, find personal info, unlock emails, then exploit the target. The repetition is not boring per se—especially if you're a fan of detective work—but it can get overwhelming in the latter half of the game.

[*] Some logic leaps. While most of the investigations are well-designed, a handful of them include solutions that feel unintuitive—like needing to click on a very specific phrase buried in a long article or assume something that’s not clearly hinted at. The lack of an in-game hint system can make these roadblocks more frustrating than they need to be.

If there is a flaw in the 7 hours/2 chapters that I've played, it's that sometimes you will be timed while searching for "key information" in a designated area. You often aren't told exactly what you're looking for, leading to, essentially, a pixel hunt where you sift through all the data as fast as you can, hoping you get lucky before time runs out. It's actually pretty effective at building tension, but failing often means a reset to a checkpoint that's JUST far back enough to be annoying, but not ruinous. I give Cyber Manhunt a middle B. It's a fun investigation game that is similar to Orwell and Analogue: A Hate Story where you piece together the plot by using "hacking," or really Hollywood-style hacking in between social engineering.

The gameplay suffers a bit for its loop, in which the majority of your time is spent looking through in-game social media logs of your subjects. That's a fun premise, but the game proceeds by having you click on relevant lines of text. When you hover your cursor over lines you can "collect" to add to your case file, the lines turn red, but otherwise there is no indication which bits are relevant. There are many times early on I just missed the lines in question, and so I spent the last few chapter meticulously mousing over EVERYTHING so I didn't miss anything, but I STILL missed things. It was a little frustrating and I had to use a guide a couple times to find what I had overlooked, even though I read everything.

More frustrating than that though are the mini-games. Usually when doing something more intense than reading, you're playing a mini-game to hack a system or reason out a situation. For the most part these mini-games aren't difficult and I appreciate the variety. However, in later chapters the mini-games start getting time limits, and some of these are unnecessarily harsh. A particular hacking mini-game in Chapter 5 nearly made me rage quit, and even with a video tutorial from YouTube, I was really struggling to get past it. Maybe I'm just a slow reader, but I think it's just less-than-good game design.

The developer seemed to understand those criticisms too because in the Home Sweet Home DLC there aren't any time limits, and in Hello World there is only one mini-game with a time limit that's [i]incredibly[/i] generous. Also in the DLCs, the mini-games can be straight up skipped. I wish that had been in the base game.

Luckily, all mini-games and gameplay loop tedium are absolutely overshadowed by the excellent story. All seven chapters (DLC included) had great twists and turns. All the cases are connected in subtle ways, and almost no one ended up how they began. All the characters were complex, and the writers absolutely nailed social media posts, including strangers of all genders uncomfortably randomly hitting on strangers in their own feeds. And what starts off as a "simple" matter of investigation eventually spirals into sci-fi and metaphysical questions. I loved it.

The English translation is unfortunately wonky, and there are typos or "just doesn't sound right" issues in just about every other sentence. There's also some polish issues where the voice acting doesn't quite match up with what's on the screen, like the script changed after the line were recorded. Even so, the translation is good enough that you can follow what's going on and there's nothing more egregious than mixing up pronouns. But man, if the story had been run through a native English speaker/writer before being released, this would have been an [i]incredible[/i] story.

The music is awesome as well, and really sets the mood, but the story really caries the game. I'm excited to try the sequel now, though I'm hoping the gameplay loop for Cyber Manhunt 2 is less tedious.

I would like to first thank the dev for this game and for having taken the time to translate the game  (whatever may be the tools used for it) so we, non-chinese players, could venture into your universe. I've bought this game along with its DLC and the second game that is currently in Early access (I'll start that one when I've got some time).

But let's jump in the meat of the review. 

1)  I can't start without addressing the main issue of this game, for us non-chinese readers/speakers : the translation. Many things have been said about it and while the two DLC's do display a better text than the main game, let's be honest and say that it's the major con of the software. 

I would like to tone this concern down in regard with my earlier praise to the dev for translating it, but nonetheless it led me to check for guides on Steam and videos on youtube to solve some problems that were either due to a vague translation or to more problematic issues as I'll develop below.

2) Voice acting.... not necessary and not very welcome either. You've got a range of icons to tell us that we're listening to a phone call, it's not like we need to listen to anything in particular. Let's take the good examples of Orwell and Song of Farca that don't have any voice acting and yet have a great atmosphere, great writing, etc. And also, no option to mute voices only, Or you mute all the sounds (music being dealt with apart from it) or you have to listen to .... quite robotic or emotionless or otherwise misplayed dialogues. Again, DLC's level up the game a little more on that matter.

3) My main concern is definitely the lack of "respect" that I felt sometimes during the game. I understand that the dev team is very small, but then select what you display on screen, please. And make it, if not useful, at least usable. 
   - many web articles are just there for lore purpose, nothing else ;
   - tapped phone calls received through mail are not always usable to make the case progress ; 
   - some hinted leads are dead ends from the start, no way to investigate them ;
   - No way to direct call people we know the phone numbers.... ;
   - Sometimes, the chuncks of info that you have to select make little sense, mostly due to the translation. Why should I 
      select an obvious conclusion to a drama (for instance : "I'm alone in the world now that they're gone") and not the fact 
      themselves (for example : "They died in a car accident last month") ? ;
      Ok, it's not always that simplistic, but it's sometimes the case and in the end, it becomes more of a clicker game where 
      you hunt down info at random than an actual investigation. Again, respect your player intelligence or try to have a 
      better translated and adapted script, because while I'm grateful to you for your effort, it was a bit underwhelming...;
   - maybe my main grip here : you often have to select the information in a particular document and not anywhere else. 
      And that is a huge concern of mine. Let's say you see that NPC 1 got divorced while skimming through a web article. You could extract the data here and add it to the share folder, right ? No, you will have to wait for the same info to appear on an obscure Darknet-ish forum or on social medias, etc. Which is.... not unseen before but still annoying. 

Do respect your players. Be conscious of your own limitations and restrict our freedom of action right from the start instead of giving us the illusion of "freedom of action". Again, not unseen before in this kind of games and others genres. Indeed, it has been a recurring pattern since the beginning of gaming, but... maybe there are elegant ways to deal with it. Again, Orwell dealt with it quite nicely by focusing on what was relevant for us, for the story, for the game. Another thing that can be done is letting us "phone" the characters and just letting them or not answering, or blocking us, or just repeating the same automatic response. It would still tell us that it is a dead end, but at least we wouldn't feel like heavily disabled persons unable to put 2 and 2 and take action. 

4) Good writing, good story, good characters. I liked all the cases and the general story. Nothing new under the sky, but well done. The themes were indeed a bit stressful and character writing was deep enough for me to like/love/dislike/hate them and how corrupt or mischievous they can be. Good thriller all in all. Maybe the last DLC was a bit underwhelming. the tower-defence mini-game was interesting though !

5) Music, like voice acting, was a bit redundant, I quickly muted it and put my own in the background. The problem was the same with Song of Farca but at least you could change the track before muting it completely. Orwell did handle it better with a soft lift-like music. 


Ok, I talked too much.

TL;DR => buy it both because it's a good game and to support its dev(s). Despite the caveats I mentioned, I still mostly enjoyed my journey in this universe and will launch the second game when I get time. both gameplay DLC (the only paid DLC, that is) are of good value. "Home Sweet Home" being the better story-wise and the second DLC being better gameplay-wise (because of the mini tower-defence game ^^). 

Regards

A great, story-focused hacking/detective game. Some of the translation can be off and it did affect me solving some of the more obtuse puzzles, but with a guide on the side, I found playing through the main campaign and two DLC campaigns to be a fantastic way to spend 20 hours or so.

Yes, just like other reviewers have said, if you like Orwell you will like this and really should pick it up.  Be warned though, if you're pessimistic about the direction of human society, this WILL reinforce those opinions, and many of the characters are so grotesquely evil and self-interested that it makes you question what justice for such people really looks like, and no matter what happens to them you know you cannot ever undo the damage these people have inflicted.

Unlike Orwell, each mission is a self-contained story, but some of the characters pop up in multiple missions and have ongoing character development throughout the game.

Also, it is a fair bit more difficult than Orwell.  There is an option to turn-off auto-highlighting of clues (the things that Orwell calls "data chunks") in the text so that you have to find them yourself, and you have to be VERY observant and notice things in the text and images that the game does not require you to specifically capture and does not specifically point out to you, but will crop up at a future point.  For example, you might have to phone a character to obtain extra information to progress the story, and you will have to use ALL the information you've read/seen in pictures about them  about them to get them to spill the beans.  There are various timed puzzles too, that are difficult to the point of erring on the side of unfair, but the game does allow you to re-attempt failed hacks so it's not a game-over, restart the mission at these points, which I appreciated!

Finally, yes, as others have mentioned, the English translation is not always good, but it wasn't so bad that it spoiled the game for me, and it is always clear to me what the story is trying to tell me.  More of a problem is some of the voice acting, which is a mixed bag.  Some of the actors are convincing, many are not.  I absolutely hated the voice actor for Austin Hill, in the mission "The Evidence Vanishes," and to be honest, it broke the immersion for me. * There's also some comically bad voice acting at times. To make matters worse YOU CAN'T FUCKING SKIP the spoken dialogue scenes. This is particularly egregious because in many sections you have to listen to entire conversations before you can collect any of the evidence (that is, click every sentence trying to find what will be highlighted in red as clues). 
* At some points, you're asked to piece together what happens, but you CAN'T TAB BACK TO WHERE THE INFO YOU COLLECTED IS STORED TO FIND THOSE ANSWERS!
* While it can be satisfying to poke around to get the info you need in the investigation stages, some of the other minigames/puzzles are just not fun to play. It's a very low cost game, and I did get some fun out of it--but I don't think I can, in good conscience, recommend it to others.

review:
[h1] 8/10 [/h1]

Although Cyber Manhunt may appear to be a hacking simulation game, I believe it is more appropriate to call it a social engineering simulation game. Overall, the strengths and weaknesses of Cyber Manhunt are quite evident: it has an outstanding and thought-provoking storyline that is both contemporary and ironic, with significant real-world implications. However, its gameplay design may not satisfy all players.

If you do not know social engineering, this game can give you a glimpse into the popular social science of gathering information about others through various means. By unraveling the secrets and events behind each character through information gathered from various social media platforms, websites, emails, phone calls, and more, players can engage in activities such as hacking, deception, and disguises to gather intelligence. For players who enjoy puzzle-solving and have patience, Cyber Manhunt can provide an excellent gaming experience. Additionally, the game's storyline is quite deep, depicting various cybercrimes, school bullying, exchange of interests, and blackmail. The game connects the characters through numerous fragmented yet interconnected clues, presenting players with a captivating narrative filled with criticism, irony, reflection, and depth. It is definitely worth a try for any narrative game enthusiast.

The shortcomings of the game primarily lie in its gameplay design. The game itself is relatively short, and the process of collecting clues through mouse clicks takes up a significant portion of the gameplay time. Many puzzle mini-games added to enrich the game's content may not be particularly interesting. Although they diversify the gameplay, some players may find them off-putting. Players familiar with social engineering may also feel that the game's gameplay design and certain plot developments are somewhat contrived. Furthermore, the game's depiction of hacking techniques is rushed and lacks rigor.

Overall, Cyber Manhunt surprised me beyond expectations. I recommend it to those interested in social engineering but with limited knowledge, fans of realism, and enthusiasts of text-based adventure games. If you can accept its shortcomings, you will find that Cyber Manhunt offers great value. On the contrary, if you are not interested in its gameplay and storyline, there is no need to give it a try. It is worth noting that this game draws heavily on Osmotic Studios' Orwell series released in 2016, with the main difference being that this game focuses more on narrative description and characterization, while Orwell offers a stronger interactive gaming experience.

review:
I normally avoid leaving negative reviews on games that didn't work for me. The way I see it, my personal dislike of particular features or plot points doesn't necessarily add up to a bad game for someone else. Unfortunately, in the case of Cyber Manhunt, I feel justified in leaving this review because I think the game fails at what it sets out to do: making the player feel like a hacker solving a compelling mystery.

The first, and perhaps greatest challenge to immersion I encountered here is the writing. To clarify, my primary issue is not with the English translation. I do believe there are many odd choices that add up to very stilted and unnatural-sounding conversations, but I would have been able to see past this if the characters and stories involved were more thoughtfully written to begin with. 

Most of the characters you investigate in Cyber Manhunt embody one-dimensional stereotypes. This makes the stories you uncover about them highly predictable. The social issues the game claims to focus on (according to the blurb: cyber violence and privacy breaches) are explored in what I personally believe to be an equally shallow, one-dimensional way. There are also additional social issues, such as sexual violence and human trafficking, which I believe the writers were simply not equipped to handle at all—and I say that as someone who has had to deal with these issues in my past work. The behaviour of both the victims and the perpetrators is painfully unrealistic, to the point that I suspect the writers took more inspiration from internet creepypastas than real life cases. 

Because the puzzles rely on narrative complexity to be interesting, I believe the game falls flat on this front as well. You scour social media accounts, emails and webpages for names and other personally identifiable information. Databases and password cracking tools help you access more data to scour. There are occasionally phishing sequences where you select dialogue choices. All of these mechanics have the potential to be a fun, highly simplified social hacking simulation, and I can see Cyber Manhunt is trying its best to do just that. I even believe it might have worked—if there was more thought put into how the characters communicate and what their motivations might be as full-fledged human beings. A predictable story with one-dimensional characters who speak and write in a stilted, unnatural sounding way just doesn't make for a very engaging data-scouring experience.

All in all, I am disappointed with the wasted potential in Cyber Manhunt. I hope that if the devs go on to make more narrative games, they will make quality writing a higher priority of the overall experience.

I had a good time playing this game. I've never played any input-based type experience in which you feel like you are scouring the web for information, learning about people's secrets, logging into their accounts, etc. and I really liked feeling like I was immersed in what I was doing and in all the info I was collecting. 
However, I would say I would only recommend this game to people that aren't looking for some in-depth hacking simulator. A few critiques I have are that some of the clues are very easy to scroll over and not collect, which made me want to look up a guide for a lot of the sequences. I tried to do the majority on my own, but towards the end of the game especially, I was heavily leaning on online guides to know what to do. But with that being said I am REALLY bad at puzzles and have little patience, so maybe take that part with a grain of salt. 
Also, the translations and awkwardness of the dialogue in this game is very prominent. It can be a bit jarring to have such a graphically unique and interesting game have those awkward dialogue moments that a lot of the time didn't make complete sense. But if you can look past those issues and just have fun hacking away, it's a fun game at its core and you can tell that the developers put a lot of love and effort into it. 


All in all, it held my attention as a destressor from everyday life (besides the minigames, which I wasn't good at, so they kind of stressed me out. lmao). I might return and play the DLC sometime. I don't think I'm invested enough to collect all of the achievements.

review:
First and foremost, this is NOT a hacking game. It is a hacking THEMED puzzle game. It's one of those types of hacking games where there's clearly a specific path forward, but the technology in-game is not consistent with the real world so you're forced to act as the game expects and not rely on your technical expertise or intuition. This might be fine for people who don't know anything about computers, though, but I have worked in IT for over 20 years and find this extremely aggravating as I enjoy actual hacking games and detective/mystery stories where I can put that to use. It doesn't need to be literally analogous to the real world, but there's a certain aptitude you develop in IT that aids you in trying to figure things out and none of that is applicable here. 

For example, email addresses unrelated to what you're doing are masked, which is not consistent with the platform since you can see related emails. You have the ability to search using the resources provided (search engine, database), but you can't search for emails that the game doesn't want you to search for, even though it's directly related to the task at hand and would be a way to get the solution you're looking for in the real world. Another example, in the tutorial mission, I accidentally skipped past a point of dialogue where the woman has given you the next task, but since the game is presented very rigidly I can't for the life of me figure out what the game is looking for, and your hands are tied despite having the "web" and database to search through. Searching the "web" only works when it's extremely specific to the case, and searching an email address should pull up a ton of info but this is not an option due to it not being what the game is specifically expecting. Anyone familiar with technology would be able to tell you that there's always multiple ways to get the information, but the game does not allow for this. It's a puzzle to figure out, not hacking. As far as hacking goes, it was a stereotypical fantasy magically-get-the-answer thing to click. No technical knowledge needed, and in my case it worked against me.

The translations or pronunciations of technical jargon are off, enough to also be aggravating if you're familiar with the terms. Non-tech folks likely won't notice, but it makes me wonder who the game's target audience is? Games like these should be about immersion, and they snap you out of it quickly and it's very obvious that this is in no way related to hacking or the tech industry.

I have no idea why this game is rated so highly. I picked this up because I love hacking and mystery games, and this had almost 10k positive reviews. After playing for just a few minutes it was the complete opposite of what I was expecting in an entirely negative way. It reminds me of Orwell, but Orwell had much better presentation and design and wasn't trying to be something it's not. I actually enjoyed Orwell a lot but it was clear it was in the Orwell fantasy world, so it was logically consistent. This game mimics real world applications in a way that is completely misleading and jarring, and equally inconsistent. 

Do some heavy research before purchase. If you're technical, hard pass, there's too much suspension of disbelief and plenty of other hacking games to choose from that are better suited. If you're not technical, and you enjoy puzzles and the idea of movie hacking, you might like it.

6/10 Decent.

It's an okay investigation game, where you basically act through a computer terminal and utilise database tools to compile profile/evidence.

Sometimes you'll 'phish' someone with link to get their phone information, sometimes you'll call them and impersonate someone to steal information etc, it's all very simplistic, like a rudimentary version of Orwell (similar themes really).

So, if you liked Orwell, you'll probably enjoy this one.

The downsides?

The translation is iffy, there's a lot of broken English, some atrocious pronunciation (dahtah (for data) and yet they say database absolutely fine?), and dialogue always doesn't flow very well. 

The game is also keen to throw one off mechanics at you that never crop up again, rather than focus on the fundamentals of the investigation story ~ you can also sequence break by accident, which can skew the flow of the narrative as well.

It's nothing like Ace Attorney series as one review has misleadingly pointed out ~ you're not presenting evidence, cross examining witnesses, or coming to any conclusions on a regular basis, or even at all. You're essentially collecting data as a whole and then submitting it as a data sheet. You never, ever, come to any conclusions within the game or within any the cases in the game. You go round hunting information and clues and submitting it to your boss, who makes any inferences etc, but you, yourself won't have anything to do with this.

You also won't have any sway in changing the outcomes; You can't wrongfully accuse anyone or anything like that, it's a very linear investigative information collation game ~ and that's absolutely fine, it works, it's an enjoyable one with a bit of a try hard story and bad English, and it's worth it for £5 or whatever it goes for on sale. 

But please, don't come into this game thinking you have much power to change things (beyond the ending), don't come in thinking this is an indie Ace Attorney sort of game, it's nowhere near in terms of mechanics or otherwise.

Do I recommend it? Based on the price, yes. I think the pricing is absolutely fair for what they're offering. If you can put up with some broken English, you'll be fine playing through this one.

review:
Long story short - this is a really good game that lacks a lot of polish and has plenty of bugs. If you can look past that and appreciate the gameplay and the surprisingly accurate portrayals of hacking tactics, then you will find PLENTY to enjoy in this game.

First, I want to praise the game for its portrayal of hacking and the steps that make it possible. It's simple to grasp and communicates the very real threat of phishing and social engineering while keeping things entertaining. The opening title cards of the game say that this was one of their biggest reasons for making the game. In that respect, they 100% succeeded. If you are looking for a game that accurately and easily explains hacking, this is the best example I can think of.

As for the game loop, there are many similarities to the Ace Attorney/Phoenix Wright games.

- you are a given a small handful of clues
- you enter an investigation segment where you search for more clues/information by clicking on everything you see (just like Ace Attorney)
- you take your findings and confront someone, similar to cross-examinations in Ace Attorney
- you go through a [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mvDspWLhPhg] "Revisualization Sequence" [/url] and gather all the information you have to label somebody as killer/witness/hacker/etc
- repeat

This game loop works well and definitely encourages exploration, as any failures or mistakes made along the way will only send you back a few minutes at most, and usually only a few seconds. It also helps that the game focuses on depth rather than a wide variety of mechanics. There are many different minigames along the way, but they are usually one-offs or done a few times back to back. The core game mechanics are a small set and persist throughout the game. These mechanics are fairly open-ended, so the flexibility you have to work with his rather high. And what's more - the game often chains mechanics together to really test your mental flexibility. Sometimes, it can feel cheap - as in brute force would be a more efficient method than logic, but it rarely ever gets that bad.

That said, the game does have issues with polish. It's actually very similar to Ace Attorney where you have to select the exact piece of evidence that the game wants, regardless of how close or relevant the one you chose actually is. Other times, the game has race conditions that occur that don't exactly softlock the game, but certainly glitch it out and make it hard to progress. While I have never been softlocked in this game, I have run into glitches that force me to fail time sensitive tasks. And regardless, several people have reported softlocks exist in this game, so it's something to beware of.

Also, the UI is a bit finnicky. The primary UI you will be working with is meant to look like a computer desktop, which is really cool and makes a great backdrop for the rest of the game, but there are definitely some cut corners. For example, you cannot use your scroll wheel to scroll through content - you must click and drag the page or the scroll bar. That got annoying fast, but I got over it. Also, similar to Ace Attorney, investigation segments will involve you hovering over everything and anything you see until your cursor (or in this case, the background) changes to signify that a clue is here. This makes the process of finding clues a bit repetitive, even though the game throws a few new mechanics in for each chapter. And I could be wrong, but I am fairly certain that the color-change-on-hover mechanic has a weird hover detection, leading to false negatives. I am not sure, and even if it is the case, it is rare - maybe once or twice a chapter.

The story is surprisingly engaging. For starters, it is a fairly mature game, as it delves into some pretty painful and disgusting subject matter. Examples include permanent bodily injury and human trafficking. The game uses these subjects to explain the threat and danger of an insecure internet and how people exploit it for their benefit. We see recurring characters who struggle with these threats and dangers and feel the pull to use the elements for their own purposes. Seeing the struggle really makes the story feel impactful, real, and threatening, while not running into any form of power creep. The conflicts are unique, but self-contained. The characters grow and develop as the story progresses.

It's a bit difficult to say whether or not characters have depth. Technically, they have a lot of depth, but most of their depth is literally given to the player as bullet points on a board highlighting what the character went through. As more bullets are added, their motivations get further explained and then their justifications become revealed. In that light, I'd say almost every character we come across has depth and purpose for being in the story. But that said, it's still just bullet points on a page - there's a chance that the characters will feel cheap since their traits are rarely revealed through dialogue or conversation.

And on that note, it's important to say that the English version of the game is full of typos, bad grammar, run-on sentences, and otherwise broken english. And I don't mean once every few minutes. I mean multiple times per paragraph - sometimes, multiple times per sentence. It's clear that this game was translated into English, but not very well. The text is perfectly understandable, so I am not bothered at all by it, but I imagine others might.

As for the voice acting, most reviews seem to dislike the voices or find them passable, but I thought all of these voice actors did a phenomenal job. I was actually shocked at how good some of these portrayals were. The voices didn't just add another dimension, they actually communicated character traits that the text and story alone could not. For example, Van's voice actor really highlighted just how unhinged the character was - something that the story alone doesn't clearly portray. Another example is Coral's voice actor communicating shame and embarrassment on top of the fear that the text displayed. Every single voice was great, but special praise to the voice actors for Ashley, Van, and Quiller.

The music is surprisingly well done, but there aren't a wide variety of songs. The art has 2 styles - the computer desktop/applications and the people/locations. The desktop/applications are sleek and beautiful. The locales/characters are emotive and detailed. Character animations are a bit static/stiff, but I feel it adds to the charm.

All in all, I had a great time with the game. I finished it at 40 hours, but that was with me taking the long way around and digging through everything. This is more like a 5-15 hour game, depending on how much you guess right the first time. I enjoyed the accurate portrayal of hacking, the story, music, art, and mechanics. I got annoyed with glitches, but they were usually easy to resolve or easy to recover from.

review: The entire plot of this plot-heavy game is conveyed through an extremely poor English translation. Normally I wouldn't mind, but it's a pretty huge issue in this game for two reasons: 1) You rely on information provided through dialogue to progress through the game, and 2) the game deals with very sensitive subject matter like rape. I genuinely felt bad for the voice actors who were attempting to read such a stilted and awkward script as seriously as possible. There's also a ton of little places you can screw-up that can cause you to repetitively have to reload and retry things again and again, which is exhausting when you can't just skip through dialogue.

I rarely post negative reviews cause I usually pick the games I buy very carefully. I was looking for a fun hacking game though and with the limited selection out there I chose this based on its "Very positive" user reviews. I was actually going to give it a thumbs up too, until I actually read the question Steam asks:
"Would you recommend this game to other players".
To that specific question I would definitely have to say: No.
It's tough, cause I kinda like the game, I just wouldn't expect other players or a friend to have the amount of patience with it that I've had. Subjectively, I'd score it a 7/10, objectively I'd give it a 4/10.

TL;DR The game sets you up for failure. Timers on puzzles mean replaying sections where you fail to solve the puzzle on time, which in some cases are virtually impossible to do on your first try. Then short cutting the info gathering to buy time on your next try, because you already have the info in your head, sometimes introduces game breaking bugs. All this also pushes the player towards walkthroughs completely ruining the experience. Game also has some immersion breaking unnatural language issues.

PROS:
- Interesting story with some good twists.
- Immersive. You can really get into following along with the stories of the people you "hack" and the hacking makes you feel empowered.
- Valuable message around personal data, AI and social media in general.
- A few fun, innovative puzzles.
- Well made UI and visuals (Nothing special, but not bad)

CONS:
- Convoluted puzzles. Some puzzles require you to assume things that aren't intuitive. Like having to use concatenated dates as a password but not being told that specific parts of the dates need to be left out. Having these on a timer seriously exasperates the problem.
- Language issues. Whoever wrote the script and content for this game is definitely not a natural English speaker. All the spelling is correct but the grammar is flawed and the manner of speaking is jarringly foreign. Like everything was written in Japanese and then run through Google translate or something. Unnecessary extra words in places and weird grammar immediately make you feel like "This is not the way people speak". It's honestly quite immersion breaking in a game that involves a lot of reading.
- One or two bugs. Mostly the game runs just fine, in fact you could pretty much run it on a potato. I literally only encountered one bug, but it was game breaking and required that I reload which lost me some progress. The biggest issue about it is that it was caused by trying to short cut problems with the first con I mentioned meaning that alleviating the biggest issue of the game isn't an option.

The translation is so poor that you simply can't deduce some puzzles and have to go with trial and error. Other times it refers to people by the wrong name or gender, further confusing things. As some segments are timed this leads to a frustrating and ultimately boring experience. This game wants to be "Orwell" but fails. It would take a rewrite and re-record of the voiceover to fix it.

Cyber Manhunt is a comprehensive internet sleuth game from Chinese developers, Aluba Studio. Players must search the darkest online corners to discover pivotal information. Similar to the [i]Orwell[/i] games but with a more sinister story, the title is sure to appease fans of the genre. However, it is not without its flaws and unfortunately suffers from lacklustre text due to its abysmally poor translation.

[b] [u]Pros[/u] [/b]
[list]
    [*] 5 extensive chapters that are all cleverly entwined.
    [*] Differing endings.
    [*] Inventive puzzles & minigames throughout.
    [*] Covers grim themes of crime and corruption.
    [*] Pleasant & simple user interface.
[/list]

[b] [u]Cons[/u] [/b]
[list]
    [*] Awful translation to English, dialogue can come across as robotic and insincere.
    [*] Cumbersome text scenes which do not flow naturally.
    [*] Lacks explanation of puzzle mechanics.
[/list]

[h1]Story: Malignant Data Corruption & Cybersecurity[/h1]
Cyber Manhunt features 5 extensive chapters which range from 1-3 hours each, depending on personal playstyle. Each chapter tackles new persons of interest and a seemingly unrelated story which all comes together upon completion of the game. The stories do feature quite sensitive themes including rape, bullying, female slave imprisonment and more. Whilst there is not any graphic imagery or descriptions, most of the chapters will centre around these topics. Thus, it is important for potential buyers to be aware that it is not an easy-going hacking game and is quite serious in nature.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2544733102

Players begin working for Titan, a large data storage company that can access unlimited personal information about the citizens of Allivia. Our job is to track down specific material to uncover the answers Titan seeks, typically involved in crime investigations or missing persons. The game purposefully questions the indefinite power of having easy access to this data and focuses on the consequences. Moral questions begin to arise, are we helping citizens or doing more damage than good? What is the goal of Titan? Is it something to be proud of?

Soon enough, the corruption can no longer be ignored and a self-proclaimed prophetic persona appears with vengeance for large data companies. Putting Titan in a negative spotlight and allowing players to shape the final acts.

[b] [u]Translation Issues[/u] [/b]
Unfortunately, the biggest disappointment of Cyber Manhunt was its poor translation. Although everything "made sense" and I knew what was going on, the general flow of dialogue was poorly executed. It was easily recognisable that some sections were a direct translation to English and sounded robotic. There were also an abundance of grammar issues and just misspellings such as "CIO" (CEO), "Browbe" (bribe?). Typically, I would not be too bothered as I enjoyed the gameplay immensely, but in a text-based online investigative game, it vastly impacted the games entirety and diminished the serious themes the developers attempt to convey. Some conversations were just laughable and came across as extremely fake. I understand that the Chinese developers are not native English speakers and the Indie nature of the title may prevent proper translation due to funding/time constraints, but it really was abysmal in parts, considering dialogue and text are the sole premise of the title. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2546018709

[h1]Gameplay: Online Investigations, Puzzles & Minigames[/h1]
Majority of the game will be spent on a simple computer interface with access to very familiar applications, "Toothbook", "Gogo" and more. Players must use these programs to uncover information about a specific person. At the beginning of each chapter, we are typically only given the person’s name and a few bits of information. The name can be pasted into "Gogo" to find their "Toothbook" which will unveil their nicknames, hobbies, marital status, friends and so forth, furthering the investigation. This information is all collated into their profiles.

Useful information will be highlighted in red once the cursor scrolls over it, signalling that it can be collected. There are also a handful of other useful applications which can be used as phishing or anonymous calling. Once private information such as DOB is revealed, this can be used in the "Crack" program to obtain passwords. Essentially, keep finding more information which will unlock access to more pertinent data needed to complete the chapter. I found the data-collection to be much more complex than I had originally thought, with lots of different accounts, programs and areas to explore, it was difficult to keep track of it all. But this is in no way a criticism, I enjoyed the more challenging approach and it gave me a sense of achievement when new clues were discovered.

Scour through webpages, emails, private chats and assemble the clues to reveal the full story. There are 4 goals within each chapter and when one goal is fulfilled to 100%, players can enter "reasoning" mode which is essentially a minigame (which differs each time) that puts the story in chronological order and makes sense of all data already obtained.

[b] [u]Minigames & Puzzles[/u] [/b]
Despite this style of game being somewhat monotonous in design and virtually boils down to information-finding, it does include a myriad of minigames to spice things up. Minigames include "hacking" scenes with specific order-based puzzles, matching symbols in a designated layout. Another example was a more strategy-focused section where players must control the popularity of media articles in each state of the country. I found most of these puzzles to be rather inventive and thought-provoking, without succumbing to lazy mechanics or overusing the same concepts, it was kept fresh and interesting.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2548412313

Where this section failed was in its explanation of these puzzles. Sometimes there was a seemingly in-depth cinematic description of what was required, yet it was executed poorly and ultimately caused even more confusion. Other times, no attempt at an explanation was made and I was left with a daunting map filled with things to interact with that I had no idea of their purpose. Even worse, majority of the puzzles are timed and without any indication of what to do (with pausing also disabled), I had to figure it out by trial and error, which was easy enough but of course wastes time and typically resulted in me having to redo the section from scratch.

[h1]Graphics & Sound[/h1]
Being a cyber/hacking simulation title, there is little to comment on in terms of graphics, but the simple interface is clean and very straightforward. There are a handful of cinematic scenes that are actually quite decent and felt reminiscent of comic style art.

Some characters are voiced, as well as calls. The voice-overs are mediocre but do their job. The foreboding soundtrack is on a loop and felt nostalgic of investigative crime TV shows, almost putting pressure on players to uncover clues faster.


[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Cyber Manhunt is an excellent online investigative game, taking inspiration from games such as [i]Orwell[/i] and [i]Papers Please[/i]. Its extensive chapters have an abundance of clues to discover, with countless puzzles and minigames to complete along the way. Despite suffering from severe translation issues which greatly impacted the dialogues flow, the gameplay holds strong and should appeal to any fans of the aforementioned titles. Taking approximately 10-14 hours to complete with differing endings and many achievements encouraging replays, for $15AUD, I highly recommend it to all who love an extensive online lurk.

Cyber Manhunt is a pretty good game. The story is well-written, if a bit difficult to follow sometimes, and has a lot of good elements to it. There are flaws, however, and many of them interfere with the immersion. This review will be free of major spoilers, with only a few plot points hinted at. I won't ruin your play experience if you decide to buy it yourself.

In terms of visuals, the game looks great. The art and animation are well done and have their own unique style to them. The UI looks pretty great too, though there are problems there that lie beyond their sleek exteriors. One of the most annoying parts (something that could have been easily implemented, I'll bet) is that you can't use the TAB key to move between fields. The password cracker requires you to input several pieces of information in across multiple fields, and you'll do this several times in each case. You can't use TAB, though, so you pretty much have to do everything with your mouse. It's a minor gripe, but I found myself annoyed at these sections of the game. They included CTRL+C and CTRL+V, but not TAB?

Sound design is mixed. The music is great, from the actual lyrical songs, to the general background music. It's a little repetitive, but it fits the game and doesn't distract from what you're trying to do. I think the Reasoning music is my favorite just for how nice it sounds, adding a bit of urgency to the normal background music. The voice acting, however, is mixed at best. Some roles sound better than others, but the game would have benefited from better voice direction.

However, the story suffers the most, because whoever was in charge of localizing the game [i]seriously dropped the ball[/i]. The tutorial and first case (so the content included in the demo) have the best localization, but even then it's not great. The wording of hundreds of messages in the game is awkward and fake-sounding, some parts even sounding like those phishing e-mails written by the prince of Nigeria. There were places where the localization was downright unintelligible, and I ended up having to make guesses in certain parts of the game to progress the story because I couldn't make sense of the options provided.

The story itself, localization issues aside, is good, but feels disjointed at times. There are two major plots that run simultaneously, and they seem completely separate from each other, even when they should be working together. Also, characterization for the main NPC was just wrong - through other dialogue and flavor text, the game seems to be trying to establish this character as your friend, but they act distant at best and antagonistic at worst, so your motivations get muddled at certain parts of the story. Puzzle design is pretty good, though there are two or three puzzles that will practically force you to look up a guide because their design is pretty obtuse. But overall, the game has a good message about privacy in the digital age - it's just a bit hampered by the way the game is presented.

Overall, Cyber Manhunt is a good, but flawed game. After playing other hacking games like Code7, Hacknet, and Uplink, I found it to be more on the point-and-click adventure side of things rather than an actual hacking simulator, but it really needed a final layer of polish if it wanted to be one of the greats in the genre. I think the game's overall appeal would be greatly increased by having a good localization team go through and fix a lot of the rough translations and making the game more accessible and immersive.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
You work for [i]Titan[/i], one of the big companies in [i]Allivia[/i]. Your job? Looking for people's information on the internet. [b]Cyber Manhunt[/b] is a game that will show you the dark side of the internet from leaving your personal information everywhere.

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 5 chapters
- Minigames and riddles on some chapters
- All voices are dubbed

[b]Cons:[/b]
- Some riddles are too vague to solve
- Most timed events are too short, relying you on retrying the event again to get the job done

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you are looking for other games that look like [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/491950/Orwell_Keeping_an_Eye_On_You/][b]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/b][/url] ([url=https://steamcommunity.com/profiles/76561198132503739/recommended/491950]my review[/url]), buy this game at a sale.[/i]

[hr][/hr]
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h3]Graphics[/h3]
The game uses a similar design as the [i]Mac[/i] operating system. A list of applications is available at the bottom of the screen, centered with some additional info such as news, objectives, and collected information on each corner of the screen. Although the game incorporates applications and websites that you usually use every day, some applications are also specifically designed for the game. However, they are not maximized, leaving a lot of empty spaces behind. Some people with reading difficulties might benefit from the use of space and bigger text, especially the browser.

[h3]Story[/h3]
The story is divided into 5 chapters, each with a different focus in mind. You'll investigate different people in each chapter except for a few characters that will appear in more than one chapters, connecting their involvement in a bigger picture. While you'll benefit more from the story by remembering these reoccurring characters, each chapter can still be enjoyed separately.

Some cutscenes are also introduced between each chapter, focusing on you and the company that you worked in. Everything will be wrapped up in the ending, which is also connected with the conclusion of the last chapter. While the story might come as a surprise to some people, it didn't affect me much since I played a game with a similar concept before. However, some parts of the story feel a bit odd, mostly due to the translation and different dialogue choices in the game.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2421076473 

[h3]The Game[/h3]
[b]Investigation[/b]
The main feature of [b]Cyber Manhunt[/b] is a cyber investigation, where you have to collect someone’s profile by gathering information online. It tries to make it as realistic as the real world by collecting data from social media, news portals, and other websites while incorporating some fantasy elements as well. A company database is available at your disposal, which you can use to gather more detailed data from some input.

However, finding the correct information tend to be troublesome since you need to hover your mouse to the text before collecting them. Some information that seems to be useful also tends to not be collectible if the developer chooses not to make it so, turning everything into a “hovering my mouse to every sentence that I could see” game just to satisfy the condition. The game also has no clue system which might halt your progression if you accidentally miss one piece of information that is buried beneath the haystack of information.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2421076590 

The introduction of the cracking tool is also a bit ridiculous. You can put some personal information of the target on the app and voila, you'll get the target's password. The game doesn't seem to give a quick option to copy and paste all of the required info in one click though - there are 6 fields to fill, and filling them one by one every time is very tiring. Moreover, the tool only gives one password and strangely, it works for almost every account that the target uses. While this doesn't make sense, some people actually do these kinds of stuff so I'm not sure whether the game does this on purpose to remind us not to do this practice or not. 

[b]Riddles and Minigames[/b]
Some riddles are tricky and not obvious enough to solve. Although some clues are available, they tend to be confusing since you need to know various things beforehand, such as how house numbering works and the date format that the developer intended to use. The game tends to use the MMDD format for dates and I kept on using the DDMM format out of habit, which goes worse when the year is also involved. One riddle also requires you to unlock a phone with a pattern that is not possible to do in an actual phone, triggering some confusion. To make it worse, everything must be done within a time limit, which is almost impossible to accomplish on your first try.

On the other hand, I had fun playing the minigames. Some of them are similar to other puzzle games like [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/367580/Hook/][b]Hook[/b][/url], while some are more original. The tutorials that are provided before you start some minigames also help you to understand how they work. However, one minigame is quite difficult to understand, especially if you want to unlock a certain achievement.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2421077117 

[b]Length and Replayability[/b]
Steam says that I finished the game in 12.6h, while the in-game clock states that I did it in ~12.2h. Each chapter can be finished in 1-2 hours, which can take longer if you want to get some achievements. Despite the achievement mentioning three endings, two of them are similar to each other while the last one is a bad ending that will lead you to a game over screen. There is no reason to replay the game apart from unlocking achievements.

[b]Problem[/b]
You can't skip cutscenes. The game also doesn't allow you to open the menu to load your save at some point, forcing you to restart the game manually. While I usually don't mind with this, the game has a slow loading time, making achievement hunting to be annoying sometimes.

[h1]Specs[/h1]
Intel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
To be honest, I thought that the game will be similar to [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/365450/Hacknet/][b]Hacknet[/b][/url] ([url=https://steamcommunity.com/profiles/76561198132503739/recommended/365450]my review[/url]) where you have to hack into servers and steal some information. It turns out that it's more similar to [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/491950/Orwell_Keeping_an_Eye_On_You/][b]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/b][/url] ([url=https://steamcommunity.com/profiles/76561198132503739/recommended/491950]my review[/url]) and although I don't mind with the similarity, this game feels like an inferior version of that game with some additional features. It was tiring to hover my mouse on every text to find clues and doing it when I was reading the text ruins my concentration. Some translations are also a bit off and although it's still possible to understand the story, it can ruin the immersion sometimes. However, the game is still enjoyable if you are looking for a similar game to [b]Orwell[/b] and don't mind with some annoyances.

Cyber Manhunt is kind of an interesting, 90's era adventure game but set in today's social media / online internets world.

Why is it an adventure game? Well its because it has that point and click nature to it, you solve abstract puzzles but instead of checking under the rug for a key you're futzing around in a fake GUI and logging into websites searching for info on people and their personal lives.

A lot of the websites you visit has a lot of parallels in real life like Facebook and e-maiil. And your task is generally to find enough personal details of your target to be able to hack into their personal accounts. Then you piece together information to learn what happened to that person or some other nefarious thing happening in today's world. You have scandals, you have CEOs, you have missing people. And somewhat predictable twist at the end. Its Metal Gear stuff but very very very light and you barely give a crap about any of the characters at all.

The relations between the characters can almost be confusing at times cause near the end of the dozen hour campaign you're really fed up with reading all the social media, chat, and e-mails of these subjects. Much of which are complete fluff.

But since this is an adventure game you may find yourself click spamming text to see if its a vital clue to your investigation. There's not a huge amount of options so if you're lost but have all the clues its just a few clicks to see what's next, but if you don't have the clues from the text you'd be click spamming for a while.

Now when you reach the last mission, which is 5th case it gets pretty absurd. There's a lot more timed hacks or actions. There's very abstract and annoying codes you need to figure out. You didn't experience any of these new puzzles from earlier cases, so it can be very testing. I'm not going to lie, I didn't want to keep seeing a game over screen so I used walkthroughs. Guessing games aren't my thing.

That said for a 10-12 hour game its not bad. Graphics are decent and the fake GUI you use to hack and browse websites is kinda cool. So for presentation style its decent.

But the game has a stellar mystery style soundtrack - kinda like the theme to Unsolved Mysteries. Its ominous and creepy and there's just no other game out there that evokes that awesome spoopy feel. They have many different  variants, and I feel like the devs actually have a great pianist / composer among them. Though I didn't check.

So to end this review, Cyber Manhunt doesn't push the boundaries of its adventure game-inspired hacker game. It doesn't push the realism factor either, as instead of real hacking its just cheap ebay puzzles with a timer sometimes. But its soundtrack is amazing, and its affordable. Get it if you want a basic adventure game with a hacking slant and nice tunes. 4/5 Stars.

Before I leave my review of this game, I want to say that this game is vaguely similar to 'Orwell' but this branches off into a better sub-genre. The emphasis is more about the storyline and puzzles with a slightly worse UI. For reference I hated Orwell and found it to be a chore to finish but loved this. Bear in mind that this game's storyline is quite dark and although isn't incredibly graphic might cause discomfort to some.

Firstly I should note that this is from a developer from Hong Kong, so there are a few minor translation issues that remain in the game. It's about 99.9% translated but has 1 or 2 notable translations that aren't translated properly which impacts your ability to solve a clue. I had to google both of these as they made no sense and stalled me completely.

Another concern is that the game absolutely does not let you press the Escape key on your keyboard which means that chapter introduction cinematics aren't skippable and it leads to 1-2 occasions where you have to ALT+F4 because you are on a screen that you cannot escape from. Without giving spoilers, if you attempt to phone hack in chapter 2 without having the number saved you will be hard-locked on a screen asking for the phone number you don't have.

Other notable bugs include not being able to 100% chapter 3 due to a typo (which I have reported) in a name. You can complete the mission absolutely fine but you won't be able to get the steam achievement for perfecting it.

Aside from the slower pacing in the first Chapter, which is essentially a tutorial mission that you are getting in the demo, the game feels incredibly smooth. Chapters 2-4 escalate in story line with a surprisingly good plot that caught me out as these games generally have an astoundingly basic storyline. Chapter 5 was an absolute roller coaster of detective work and difficulty and really gave the game a good way to end the current allotment of the game. The plot concluded quite well but left a cliffhanger for the next instalments which tie in nicely.

The timed elements feel off in some places, I genuinely have no idea how you are supposed to solve puzzles in the time they give you and complete the sequence in full with time to finish. For most users there needs to be additional clues before you enter the timed event or possibly an extra minute or two to compensate. Although the last mission is incredibly hectic I feel that's the one place the timer is very apt for the staple endings. The "perfect ending" does require some degree of grind but it's well placed and gives an satisfying albeit frustrating end. I think it took me ~1hr to solve it and a further 10mins to execute it perfectly.

Really can't wait for any additional chapters for DLC they release. £8 for this game is very reasonable, as the re-play value outside of achievement hunting isn't really there. It's an incredibly linear game with an open ending which you can save/load to see the other outcomes.

I became intrigued by the game based upon the concept and decided to purchase it while it was still in early access, however, did not fully delve into the game until it was fully released.

[h1] Gameplay loop [/h1]
The basic principle the game follows is that you are working for a company named Titan Matrix, and are assigned cases where you need to investigate a specific person or event. This is done by investigating a person’s online presence, gathering information from for example articles, messaging services and social media. While the game might have the tag of “hacking” this game play element is reduced to using automatic tools for cracking passwords or invading someone’s phone. Most of the game play consists of the player searching for possible clues, in most of the game automatically highlighted in red while moving the cursor over them, with the notable exception starting Chapter 4 where the player can choose the play the chapter without this assisting tool. The found clues can then be used to investigate other events and uncover more of the story. As a last note, not all clues need to be found to solve a case, however finding all can show a new perspective on the story,

[h1] Story [/h1]
As stated earlier, you are working for a company named Titan Matrix. Your job is to uncover the reasons why certain events occurred during the game by investigating the people involved. The reason for this seems to be financial or even political gain for the company. Story lines from earlier chapters do pop up in the later chapters, and do play a part in the events that unfold. [spoiler] This leads to a conflict with a hacker (the main antagonist), who is seemingly doing the same thing as you and seems to know you quite well [/spoiler] For now I will leave it at this, as this is primarily a story-driven game.

[h1] Strengths [/h1]
The game has a nice design and art style with an intuitive user interface making it easy to get into. The story line despite becoming more convoluted as the game progresses manages to capture and hold the player’s attention without overstaying its welcome. The core idea is something many people can relate to, as I can imagine quite a few people fell into the rabbit hole of researching someone online.

[h1] Weaknesses [/h1]
There are a few glaring issues currently in the game. 

[b] Language [/b]
For a story driven game there are quite a few grammatical and/or spelling errors. While this seems to have improved over time this issue still persists. This can easily lead to immersion being broken, or in the worst case confusing clues halting progress. The worst offenders seem to be passwords that are based upon dates, as most of the time the format YYYY-MM-DD is used, but in rare cases a format such as MM-DD-YYYY occurs, leading to unnecessary frustration. Overall, some issues in translation can be overlooked, but the sometimes confusing clues or weird formatting of certain clues are an issue I would implore the developers to address.


[spoiler] [b] Chapter 4: Public Opinion [/b]
At the end of the fourth chapter a certain mini-game needs to be played where the goal is to sway the public opinion. After retrying this section multiple times I just made a spreadsheet noting down all the results from my inputs, and then replayed it with “perfect” inputs, and still had difficulty. This mini-game is not much of a puzzle as it is a test of endurance and trial-and-error. This mini-game is not intuitive in the slightest and unnecessarily difficult. I implore the developers to either change the set-up of this mini-game, or at the least write a better explanation for this mini-game. [/spoiler]

[b] Puzzles and phishing [/b]
While the smallest issue, I did find that the difficulty for certain puzzles are very odd. Some puzzles are incredibly easy, to the point I would hardly argue that they are even puzzles. While others can suddenly be quite difficult. Some of these more difficult puzzles are quite clever in hindsight, but when looking at a broader definition of the word and including the phishing “puzzles” these seem to sometimes lack rhyme or reason, quickly devolving into trail-and-error. Perhaps this latter part is also due to the issues with the translation. As DLC seems to be in the works currently, I would like the developers to reassess how they set-up these phishing sections, as a simple rewrite of dialogue options might not solve the issue.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
While this game is far from perfect it is an admirable attempt from a young studio. It is a fun short delve into a concept that is becoming more and more to the forefront in current day society. While I primarily focused on the flaws in this review (in an effort to help the reader know the current issues as well as bring them to the developers attention) I can wholeheartedly say that I did enjoy my time with this game and found it to be worth the couple of euros I put down for it. While the story at times predictable it did enough to lure me in and left me wanting more. I will most likely be back for the sequel/DLC.

[i]As the studio still seems to be pushing updates and fixing some of the issues this review might be updated in the future to more accurately represent the state of the game. [/i]

Honestly for an EA game, this has potential.
